activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's time, thou was used for close friends, family or people of lower rank, and sometimes as an insult, while you was the polite form for superiors and strangers.
story:
Brooke had been stuck on the same page for twenty minutes, sprawled on the floor between the poetry shelf and the front window of Mr. Santos-Reyes's bookshop. "A Midsummer Night's Sleep," she muttered, and Payton, who was flipping through a field guide two aisles over, snorted so loudly the cashier looked up.

"It's Dream," Payton called. "And Mr. Santos-Reyes says we have to paraphrase our speeches into modern English by Friday, so maybe stop insulting the play."

Brooke glared at the page. Hermia and Lysander were arguing, which was fine, but the pronouns kept shifting around like something alive. At the top of the scene Lysander said "you" to Hermia, and then, right in the middle of the fight, he switched to "thee" and "thou," then back again. She counted the switches on her fingers. Five. That couldn't be random.

"Payton, look at this." She held the book up as Payton crossed the aisle, boots squeaking. "He starts polite, then he goes thou thou thou, then when he calms down he says you again. It's like the words flip when he gets mad."

Payton squinted. "Maybe Shakespeare just mixed them up sometimes. He didn't have spellcheck."

Brooke wasn't convinced. "Feasible," she admitted, "but I don't buy it. It happens too neatly." She turned back a few pages to the scene where Hermia talks to her father. There, speaking to a stern duke, she used "you" the whole way through. But Puck, teasing a random workman in the forest, threw "thou" at him instantly. A pattern started to form: thou for friends, family, people below you, and sometimes plain insult, while you stayed polite, for superiors and strangers. If she was right, then Lysander's switches weren't noise at all. They were the fight itself, the exact moments he stopped treating her like a lady and started treating her like someone he could wound.

She read the speech again with that rule in her head, and the modern English came fast. "Basically he's saying, you've ruined my life, you're the reason I'm stuck in this woods, and every thou is a slap." She wrote it in her notebook, then tapped the margin. "For my write-up I can cite the act and scene so Mr. Santos-Reyes can check the switching himself."

"Two things," Payton said. "One, that's actually pretty great. Two, you've been sitting on that caterpillar book for an hour and there's a larva on your sleeve."

Brooke looked down. A small green larva, evidently an escapee from the nature section, was inching toward her collar. She froze, then remembered the field guide Payton had been reading. "Page ninety-two," Payton said, grinning. "It says they're harmless."

She lifted it onto a bookmark and set it on the windowsill, then picked her pen back up. At the bottom of her paraphrase she added one more line, underlined twice: Notice the thou. It's never an accident. Then she flipped to the next scene to see who insulted whom next.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
story:
Rosalie arrived at the community center an hour early, because the little library next to the gym was open, and because she had a plan. The spelling bee started at two, and she had already studied four hundred words, but her problem was not memorizing. Her problem was that English spelling made no sense to her. Why "knight" and "night"? Why "island" with an s you never hear? Someone, sometime, must have decided these things, and she wanted to know how.

She told Aedan, who was already setting up chairs in the gym, that she was going to look for the answer. "In an hour?" he said. "You can't learn the whole language in an hour."

"I don't need the whole language," Rosalie said. "I need one pattern. If spellings got settled somehow, maybe there's a way to guess the weird ones."

In the library she pulled down the oldest, heaviest book on the shelf, a reprint of a dictionary from long ago. The cover said it was Samuel Johnson's "A Dictionary of the English Language," published in 1755, and the librarian had tucked a note inside saying Johnson's dictionary helped settle how many English words were spelled. Rosalie sat down on the floor with it. So before 1755, spelling had been looser, and this one book had helped fix it. That meant the strange spellings were not random. They were choices, locked in a long time ago, one by one.

She tested her idea against her hardest words. "Colonel." Johnson's world had already fixed that one, so there was no logic to recover; she just had to know it. But "deceit" and "receipt" had the same sound spelled two ways, which meant the ei and ie words needed checking case by case. She made a quick list of ones that were probable spellings versus ones that were traps, and she found she could usually distinguish the pattern if she said the word slowly and remembered where it came from. Harlan wandered in from the gym and quizzed her with the list until her mother called her to line up.

At the microphone, round five, Ms. Torres, who was reading the words, said, "Defendant."

Rosalie almost smiled. Harlan had drilled that one twice. It ended like "independent," not like the a in "cab." "Defendant. D-E-F-E-N-D-A-N-T. Defendant."

"Correct," Ms. Torres said.

Round eight gave her "gesture," one of her trap words, and round ten gave her "yacht," which she simply knew, the way Johnson must have known it when he wrote it down. When the last boy missed "bizarre," Rosalie got it right, and the gym clapped and Aedan whooped from the back row.

Afterward she found Aedan and Harlan by the water fountain. "So who decides how words are spelled?" Harlan asked. "A judge?"

"No judge," Rosalie said. "No defendant either. Just a dictionary from 1755 that helped settle everything." She held up her worn library card. "It's due back Thursday."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: Toulmin's full model has six parts: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal.
story:
Stella spread her index cards across her grandmother's kitchen table, where the smell of lemon polish and yesterday's coffee still hung in the air. On the first three cards she had written CLAIM, EVIDENCE, WARRANT, because that was what Ms. Charles had drilled into the debate club before the weekend. "A case is a tower," Stella said to herself, "and every point needs all three bricks." Her grandmother set down a plate of warm biscuits and slid it within reach without a word.

The problem was the club's mini-tournament on Monday. Stella wanted the top speaker slot, and Sebastian wanted it just as badly, and he had already beaten her once by poking holes in her evidence until her whole argument folded. This time she intended to build something he could not knock over. So she wrote her claim in careful block letters: The school should restrict phone use to lunch periods only.

She was on her fourth evidence card when her grandmother's old radio, its brass dials cool under Stella's fingers, crackled into a music program. The conductor of the youth orchestra, the announcer said, had changed the program order so the youngest players would not have to wait through two long pieces. Stella smiled at that. She kept writing, filling cards with facts about attention and hallway collisions she had counted herself, three in one week outside the gym.

Then she found the book. It was wedged behind the encyclopedia on the shelf her grandmother kept for rainy days, a thin paperback about argument with a diagram folded inside. Stella traced the diagram with her finger and stopped. There were boxes everywhere. Claim, data, warrant, yes, but three more beside them: backing, qualifier, rebuttal. She counted twice to be sure. Six. Six parts, not three.

"Grandma, come look," Stella called. "I've been building with half the pieces." Her grandmother dried her hands on her apron and studied the diagram, then tapped the qualifier box. "That's the 'unless' box," she said. "Your grandfather used it every time he said he'd fix the fence, unless it rained." Stella laughed and grabbed a fresh card. Her warrant, that fewer phone distractions equal safer hallways, needed backing, which meant the school's own safety report. And the qualifier meant admitting her plan worked only where teachers could supervise. She wrote UNTIL THE NEW WING OPENS and underlined it.

On Monday, Sebastian stood up with his counterargument ready, the one about emergencies, and Stella laid down her rebuttal card before he finished the sentence. Amal, scoring at the side, raised both thumbs. When Ms. Charles read the ballots aloud, Stella's name was on top, and Sebastian leaned over and whispered, "Show me that diagram at lunch." Stella grinned and slid the folded paper across the desk to him.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
The smell reached the doorstep before anyone opened the door: broth, ginger, something faintly like toasted seaweed. Riley shifted the gift bag from one hand to the other. He had never been to Dastan's house before, and he had spent twenty minutes in the kitchen at home choosing what to bring, because his mother had insisted you never arrive empty-handed. He finally settled on a box of clementines, which felt safe and unremarkable.

Dastan's mother opened the door and bowed slightly, and Riley, unsure what to do, bowed back. She smiled at that. "Dinner is almost ready," she said, and Dastan grabbed Riley's sleeve and pulled him toward the kitchen, where two enormous pots steamed on the stove. "We're having ramen," Dastan said. "My mom makes it from scratch. She simmers the broth all day, and she dries her own shiitake. It's a fungus, but a good one, so don't make a face."

The noodles went into the bowls last, and Riley watched them sink beneath a translucent slice of pork and a tangle of green onion. At the table, a quiet moment of "Itadakimasu" preceded the first bite, and then something strange happened. Everyone slurped. Dastan, his mother, his father, his little sister: the noodles vanished behind loud, wet, unmistakable slurping sounds.

Riley froze with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth. At his own dinner table, slurping meant someone would say his name in that warning tone. Here, nobody glanced at anybody. His ears warmed as he tried to work out the rule. He tested it carefully, first taking a small, nearly silent mouthful. The noodles were astonishing, but he ate them stiffly, worried about the noise. Dastan noticed. "You okay?"

"Fine," Riley whispered. "Just, aren't you not supposed to slurp?"

Dastan laughed and shook his head. "Not with ramen. With ramen, slurping's fine. Noodles like this and soba too. Watch." He demonstrated, a long cheerful slurp that ended with a satisfied sigh, and his mother nodded approvingly at them both.

Riley considered the evidence: four slurping people, zero frowns, one nod of approval. The rule, he decided, ran the other way here. He lifted a tangle of noodles, took a breath, and slurped as loud as he dared. The broth seemed to taste even better that way, hotter and brighter than the quiet bites had been. Dastan raised his water glass in a small toast, and his little sister, giggling, tried to out-slurp them both.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
story:
Zachary knelt on the old picnic table in the backyard, glaring at his sketchbook. His assignment was due Monday: a street scene drawn in one-point perspective, whatever that meant. Ms. Popescu had said something about a vanishing point, then the bell had rung and everyone had stampeded out, so all he had was the word and a blank page.

He tried anyway. He drew a road as two straight parallel lines, perfectly even, going up the page. It looked like a ladder lying on its side. It looked, Louane said when she climbed over the fence, like the world's most boring ski jump.

"It's supposed to be a street," Zachary said.

"Streets get smaller," Louane said. "Far away, I mean. Everything does."

"Things don't get smaller. That would be terrifying."

Lilly arrived next, carrying a lemonade she immediately set on his pencil case. "My grandpa says he's going to retire next to a train track," she announced, "which is a weird dream, but okay." She leaned over the drawing. "He says he likes to watch the rails come together at the horizon. He sits there for hours."

"They don't come together," Zachary said. "Rails are bolted down. If they moved toward each other, every train in the country would derail."

"Then why does it look like they touch?"

Zachary opened his mouth, then closed it. He looked at his drawing, at its two stubborn parallel lines, and an idea crawled into his head. "Get the chalk," he said.

He marched to the far corner of the backyard, where the fence ran straight along the property line, and crouched down until his eye was level with the grass. The two fence posts nearest him were as wide as his hand. The ones far away, near the gate, looked thin as pencils, and the gap between the top rail and the bottom rail seemed to shrink and shrink until it nearly pinched shut. He held his thumb up at arm's length and measured. Up close, a post was three thumbs wide. At the far end, less than half a thumb. He walked the line and measured again from the middle. Halfway along, one and a half thumbs.

"The lines aren't really meeting," he said, mostly to himself. "They just look like they meet, way out there. Even though they never actually do."

"So your street," Louane said slowly, "should start fat and get skinny."

"Everything goes skinny toward one spot." Zachary ran back to the sketchbook. He put a single dot in the middle of the page and drew his road edges straight toward it, then doorlines and windowlines and rooftops all aimed at the dot like iron filings pointing at a magnet. Lilly drew the vanishing point a tiny smiley face, which was not a required component of perspective, but he let it stay.

When Ms. Popescu leaned over the fence that evening to ask about the noise, she studied the page for a long moment. "The ladder's gone," she said.

"The ladder was obsolete," Zachary said. "New design."

She smiled and pointed at the dot. "Now draw me some telephone poles that shrink, and don't let the smiley face be the sun."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
Maria spread her notes across the library table until the wood nearly disappeared under them. Her history teacher had assigned each student a primary source, an actual document from the 1800s, and Maria had chosen a settler's diary copied into a thick blue binder from the library's archives. The assignment asked one question: why did people move west? The diary answered it on every page. "The land here is poor and the prices worse," the settler had written in March. "We go where a man can own something." Rain, failed crops, debt, and a brother in Oregon saturated the pages, the same reasons repeated until Maria could recite them. Last week, in her grandmother's kitchen, she had read a letter aloud from the same binder, written by the settler's wife to her sister back east. "We crossed the river today and the children are well," the letter said. "We passed a village and traded buttons for corn. The people were kind, though we understood not one word." Maria had liked that letter best because it felt like a real voice. Her grandmother had tapped the page and asked, "What do you suppose those villagers thought of your wagon rolling past?" Maria had shrugged then. She was not shrugging now.

She sat back and looked at her outline. It was systematic, point by point, every reason matched to a diary entry, and it suddenly felt like half a map. The diary was one person's view. She flipped through the binder again, hunting for anything written by the people who already lived along the trails, and found nothing. An hour of searching the catalog brought her only more settler papers, more wagons, more Oregon. The diary would not tell her how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed had seen the same events, because it was one voice, and the other voices had never been asked into the binder. That was a fracture in her project, and she could not pretend it wasn't there.

She found Mr. Demir at the reference desk and asked whether the library held anything, anything at all, recorded from the other side of the trail. He walked her to a shelf she had never noticed and pulled down a collection of oral histories, accounts spoken by Native elders decades later and written down by their grandchildren.

Maria carried the book back to her table and added a new page to her outline. On it she wrote: "The diary shows why one family left. It does not show what the journey looked like from the village where they traded buttons for corn. A full answer needs both." She copied the shelf number for the oral histories at the bottom, then closed her notebook and slid the blue binder back into its box.

Across the table, Francois looked up from his comic. "You're smiling at a history binder."

"Found the other half of the map," Maria said, and held up the oral history book so he could see the cover.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: At the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth.
story:
Luca stood at the edge of the old rock quarry, holding a grapefruit with a pencil stabbed through it, and wished the ground would open up and swallow him, which was unlikely, since the ground here had already been opened up and turned into Ms. Sok's outdoor science classroom. In ten minutes he had to explain to the whole class why Earth's tilt causes the seasons, and his stomach felt like it had swallowed a boulder instead of a sandwich. He had budget for exactly three minutes of courage, and he'd already used two of them worrying.

"You're doing the grapefruit thing?" Emma-Rose asked, jogging over with Orion behind her, lugging the flashlight from the supply crate. "Good, because I forgot the globe at school and my guilt was getting enormous."

Luca balanced the grapefruit on a flat stone where the quarry floor was pale and dusty, the opposite of the lush green hills above them. He pushed the pencil through it at an angle, tilting it like Ms. Sok had shown them on the diagram. "Okay, so the pencil is Earth's axis. Watch." He aimed the flashlight, which Orion held steady like a tiny sun, at the middle of the fruit.

"There," Luca said. A soft oval of light sat right on the pencil line, half above it and half below. "Tilted Earth, sun hitting it straight on like this, and the top half and bottom half get the same amount of light. Same amount of light, same length of day."

"Everywhere?" Orion said.

Luca hesitated. That was the part he'd gotten wrong in his first draft, when he'd claimed the seasons came from Earth being closer to the sun in summer. Ms. Sok had circled it in red and written one word: test it. So he had tested it, at home, with a phone call to his cousin on the other side of the world. His cousin had groaned about a school project due the same week, and Luca had asked what time the sun set there. Same as at Luca's house. Same to the minute, and it was September 22.

"That's the equinox," Luca told the class a few minutes later, holding up the grapefruit while Emma-Rose beamed the flashlight. "Around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth. My cousin on the far side of the planet and me, same sunset, same day. So distance can't be what makes the seasons, or his summer would start on the same date as mine and it doesn't. It's the tilt. Tilted toward the sun, more direct light, summer. Tilted away, winter."

Ms. Sok wrote something on her clipboard. Orion leaned over to peek. "She put a star," he whispered. "A star, Luca."

Afterward, Emma-Rose handed him the flashlight. "Trade you for the grapefruit. My little brother deserves a tilted planet."

Luaca laughed and held out the fruit, pencil still crooked through its middle like a badly built umbrella.

"Deal," said Luca.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Thomas stood near the gym doors with one hand in his pocket, where he'd been holding two quarters for the coat check all week even though the coat check was free. The hallway outside the dance smelled like floor wax and fruit punch, and the bass from inside thumped so hard the trophy case buzzed against the wall. He had walked past these doors a hundred times, but tonight there was a folding table with a bowl of glow stick bracelets, and Ayana was behind it, snapping them one at a time and handing them out.

"Take one," she said. "Take three. Nobody wants them."

Thomas took one. It was a limp green tube, dark as a garden hose at night. He watched Ayana bend a blue one until it gave a tiny crack, like a knuckle popping, and light bloomed along its whole length. A sixth grader named Yohan, who had been orbiting the table for the punch bowl and come back for cookies, stopped and squinted at it.

"Where's the battery?" Yohan asked.

"There's no battery," Ayana said.

"Everything has a battery. Flashlights have batteries."

Thomas turned the green bracelet over in his fingers. No switch, no cap, no seam that looked like it hid anything electrical. He bent it slowly and felt a small snap inside, something giving way in there, and then the tube glowed between his fingers. He held it up to the hallway light and could just see, faintly, a thin sliver of broken glass moving inside the plastic when he tilted it.

"There's a little glass vial inside," he said. "I can hear the pieces. Bending it breaks the vial." He turned it toward Yohan. "The vial's got hydrogen peroxide in it. When it breaks, that mixes with other chemicals and a dye that are already in the tube."

"And then?" Yohan said.

"Then light. It's called chemiluminescence," Ayana said. "My cousin works at a science museum. That word wins you arguments."

Yohan took three bracelets and bent them all at once, holding them up like a small green-blue constellation. "No battery," he said, mostly to himself, and walked into the gym with the fierce look of someone planning to explain it to everybody.

Thomas followed him in. Near the punch bowl, a teacher wearing a lanyard was doing a dance move that could only be described as predatory, and the whole eighth grade pretended not to notice while noticing completely. Thomas held his bracelet up next to the disco ball, which was doing nothing, honestly, compared to a broken glass vial and some dye.

"Thomas!" Ayana called from the door. "You left your quarters on the table."

He went back and got them.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
Vincent's fingers hovered over the keys while the rest of the class packed up. "One more time from bar twelve," said Ms. Van Dijk, tapping her baton on the music stand. "And Vincent, watch the road this time, not just the signs."

He had been watching the signs. That was the problem. Every time he reached the word rit. in the score, he slowed down beautifully, letting the melody stretch like taffy, and then he kept crawling at that slow speed all the way to the end while Rehan's trumpet and Miles's snare drum marched on without him. Yesterday they had crashed together so badly that Miles had put his sticks down and laughed until he wheezed.

The flashback came to him mid-count: his old teacher, back in fifth grade, had once told him that sheet music was a map, not a cage. Vincent had thought that sounded extravagant at the time, like something off a poster. Now he wondered if it actually meant something.

He started bar twelve. The rit. arrived, and he slowed, sinking into the hush of it. Then his eye caught two small words printed just after the quiet section: a tempo. He had been skimming past them for a week, evading them the way he evaded the dishes at home. A tempo. Tempo meant speed. So what did the a mean? His conscience poked at him, the part that knew he should have read every marking on the page before rehearsal instead of assuming he knew it all.

"Wait," he said, still playing softly. "A tempo. Does that mean back to the original speed? Like, the rit. is only borrowing the slow part?"

"Try it and see," said Ms. Van Dijk.

Vincent lifted his hands, dropped them back onto the keys, and pushed the melody forward, back to the brisk pace from the beginning, exactly where the drums and trumpet were waiting. Rehan grinned around his mouthpiece. Miles came in clean, and for eight full bars the three of them held together, the piano swelling loud under the trumpet line, then whispering, then surging again.

They finished the piece at the same instant, and the sound rang off the risers and faded into the shelves of stacked chairs. Ms. Van Dijk lowered her baton slowly, as if she hated to let the moment go.

"Same time tomorrow," she said. "Bar twelve."

"Bar twelve," Vincent said, and penciled a tiny circle around the words a tempo.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Oil paint does not dry by water evaporating; its oil slowly reacts with oxygen in the air, so an oil painting can take days or longer to dry to the touch.
story:
Charlie had promised her grandmother a painting of the lake by the end of the week, and today was Friday, which meant she had exactly one afternoon to finish it. She set up her easel behind the craft shack, where the picnic tables were shaded by two influential old pines that everyone fought over, and squeezed out her colors. The camp store had run out of acrylic paint on Tuesday, so the counselor had handed her a box of oil paints with a shrug and a warning she hadn't really listened to.

"Is that the lake for your grandmother?" Arnav asked, sitting down across from her with his own project, a lopsided clay turtle. "Because the lake is more blue than green."

"I know that," Charlie said, mixing blue into green anyway, because in the mornings the lake did look green, and she wanted the painting to show morning. Jacoby wandered over from the dock, dripping, and stood dripping on her towel.

By lunch, Charlie had the whole painting done, sky and water and the two pines leaning toward each other. It was the best thing she had ever made, and she planned to carry it to the bus at four o'clock. She touched the edge of a cloud with one finger, just to check, and the paint came off on her skin in a shiny smudge.

"It's still wet," she said slowly, staring at her fingertip. Acrylic dried in minutes; she had counted on that. She touched a different corner, then the middle of the sky, and every spot gave her the same greasy fingerprint. She thought about the wash line behind the cabin, where wet towels hung all morning and were still damp in the shade but dry in the sun. Water left paint when it evaporated, the way it left towels. So she carried the painting into full sun and set it on the hot gravel.

An hour later it was warm but just as smudgy. Arnav crouched beside her, frowning. "Maybe it's not the water leaving," he said. "Maybe it's something else happening."

Jacoby, who had been reading the side of the paint box, held it up. "It says oil paint doesn't dry by water evaporating. The oil reacts with oxygen in the air, so it can take days or longer to dry to the touch."

"Days," Charlie repeated. "Or longer." She looked at the bus schedule pinned to the craft shack door, then at her painting, then at the sky, as if one of them might offer a better deal. Her grandmother lived two hours away, and the bus left at four.

Ms. Pierre came around the corner with an armload of frames and stopped. "Trouble?"

"My painting won't dry and I have to take it home today," Charlie said, and then, thinking fast, "unless it doesn't have to travel flat. What if it travels face up? In a box, with nothing touching the surface?" She was already measuring the inside of the empty paint box with her fingers.

Ms. Pierre raised an eyebrow, which was the closest she ever came to cheering. "There's a flat crate by the kiln, and the art fee covers it, no extra tariff."

Charlie ran for the crate, and Arnav ran beside her carrying the painting at arm's length like a pizza.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Tristan sat in the music classroom with the trumpet on his lap, staring at the three valves as if they might confess something. Mr. Lewandowski had promised that by Friday everyone would play a full scale, but that seemed impossible. Three valves. Seven notes. The math refused to work.

"How do three buttons make seven different notes?" he asked Israel, who sat beside him polishing his trombone slide.

Israel shrugged. "Maybe the trumpet just knows."

Tristan didn't buy it. He pressed the middle valve alone and blew. The note came out lower than the open one. He pressed the first valve alone. Also lower, but a different lower. Then he pressed the first and second together, and the sound dropped further still, like walking down stairs two at a time. He sat up straighter. Each valve, alone or stacked with others, made the note fall a little more. Three valves gave more than three possibilities because they could combine.

He remembered suddenly the open house in autumn, when Mr. Lewandowski had pulled a trumpet apart on the table, loops of brass tubing coiled like a sleeping snake. Tristan had been too shy to ask then. Now he raised his hand.

"Mr. Lewandowski, when you press a valve, does the air go somewhere extra?"

"Take a look." The teacher handed him the mouthpiece-end of the demonstration trumpet with the valve caps off. Tristan peered down while he pressed the second valve, and he could just see the little door inside swing shut. The air that had rushed straight through now had to detour. "Pressing a valve sends the air through an extra loop of tubing," Mr. Lewandowski said. "The air column gets longer, and the note comes out lower."

Longer column, lower note. Tristan articulated it out loud to Israel later, pressing valves as he spoke. "It's not an equation, it's more like plumbing."

"Chronic overthinker," Cohen said from the next row, grinning. "Just blow."

So Tristan blew. He started on the open note, then second valve, then first, then first and second together, climbing down and back up the scale like a ladder. The notes landed where his ear wanted them, one after another, and when he finished the full ladder Israel tapped his music stand twice, which was his highest compliment.

Tristan looked down at the three little buttons and thought, three valves, seven notes, and every one of them lived somewhere inside that coil of brass.

"Again from the top," said Mr. Lewandowski.

Tristan lifted the trumpet and pressed the second valve.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton.
story:
Brooke spread the giant printed periodic table across the kitchen table, weighting the corners with a salt shaker, a mug, and a bag of pretzels. Tomorrow Mr. Jean-Louis was giving a surprise element quiz, and whoever got the most right would get to feed the class gecko for a week. Brooke wanted that job more than she had wanted anything since the bake sale.

"Okay," she said to Celeste, who sat across from her with her shoes on the rung of the chair, "the quiz is about finding protons. Mr. Jean-Louis said the atomic number is the key, and that's the little number above each letter box thing."

Celeste leaned over the table, squinting at the rows of squares. "There are, like, a hundred of them. Where do we even start?"

"With the simplest one," Brooke said, dragging her finger along the top row until it stopped in the upper left corner. "Hydrogen. Its atomic number is one, so every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton. One. That has to be the easiest one on the whole quiz."

Celeste tapped the box. "One proton, one proton," she chanted, then grabbed a pretzel and held it up. "This is a hydrogen atom. Nom, now it's gone."

"That's not gone, that's extinct," Brooke said, and they both cracked up so hard her mom called from the hallway to ask what was so funny. Nothing, they shouted back, science.

Brooke tested herself the way she always studied: she made a rule and then checked it against the table. If the atomic number told you the protons, then carbon, with its small six in the corner, should have six protons, and oxygen should have eight. She checked the boxes again and again, whispering, "Six. Eight. One for hydrogen," until the pattern felt as solid as the kitchen floor under her feet.

Then her conscience pricked her. Boston hadn't been in class when Mr. Jean-Lois explained the numbers, because he'd been at the dentist. If she wanted the gecko job fairly, he deserved the same chance. She pulled out her phone and texted him: hydrogen is top left, atomic number one, one proton, you owe me a cookie.

The reply came fast: "two cookies. deal."

Brooke folded the periodic table into her backpack, careful with the crease so the top row stayed readable, and set the mug back on the counter. "Same time tomorrow?" Celeste asked, already stuffing pretzels into her pocket. "Same time," Brooke said, and zipped the bag shut.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A control group is treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change.
story:
Hannah stared at the bean plants on the back counter of Mr. Ross's science classroom and felt her stomach drop. Every one of the twelve pots had gotten the fertilizer, and every one of them had grown tall and green. Her poster for the science fair said the fertilizer made plants grow better, but standing there, she realized she had no way to prove it. Maybe bean plants just grew tall on their own.

Kloe leaned over the pots beside her, ruler in hand. "Eighteen centimeters. This one's nineteen. That's good, right?"

"It's good for them," Hannah said. "But good compared to what? If somebody said the fertilizer didn't matter, I couldn't refute them. I don't have any plants that didn't get any."

Elisha, who was labeling slides at the next table, looked up. "So grow some without it."

"There's no time. The fair is in two weeks." Hannah touched a leaf, then pulled her hand back as if the plant had a reflex of its own. She stared at the shelf above the counter, where Mr. Ross kept a spare packet of seeds and a stack of empty pots, and then at the clock. Bean seeds sprouted fast. Fourteen days might be enough.

Mr. Ross was watering the fern by the window. "Need something, Hannah?"

"Just pots. And permission to use the window shelf." She kept her voice steady, though her heart was thumping. "I'm starting over with a new batch. Half of them get the fertilizer, half don't. Everything else the same. Same water, same light, same everything."

He raised an eyebrow. "Interesting plan." That was all he said, which somehow made her feel taller.

She set up eight new pots along the shelf, spacing them evenly. Four got a careful pinch of fertilizer mixed into their soil; four got none. She planted two seeds in each, at the same depth, and turned every pot so its label faced perpendicular to the window, so the light hit them all the same way. She wrote a schedule on an index card and taped it to the shelf: every pot, every day, thirty milliliters of water, no more, no less.

By Friday, green loops of stem had pushed through the soil in all eight pots. Kloe measured while Hannah recorded. "Fertilized ones are averaging four centimeters," Kloe reported. "The others, three and a half." Elisha leaned in and frowned. "That's barely a difference. I thought you wanted the fertilizer to win."

"So did I," Hannah said. Then she laughed a little, surprising herself. "But that's the thing. Now I actually know. Whatever the numbers end up saying, I can back it up."

On the day before the fair, the fertilized plants stood half a centimeter taller on average. Not the dramatic win her poster had promised. Hannah crossed out her old title and wrote a new one across the top in blue marker: "Does Fertilizer Help? A Fair Test." Elisha held the poster while she taped the growth chart beside it, both columns side by side.

Kloe stepped back to look. "You know, I thought you'd quit when the old project fell apart."

"I almost did." Hannah straightened the chart's corner. "Show me the one without fertilizer again."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
At 7:04 on Tuesday night, Tyler's phone buzzed with a video Dakota had dropped in the group chat: a guy claiming his tomato plants doubled in size after one week with "MiracleGroMax Blast." Tyler had two windowsill seedlings and a science fair in nine days, and he wanted that to be true. He typed, "How do we know it was the stuff and not just sun?" Dakota answered with three shrugging emojis. Aiden wrote, "Just try it and see if your plants get huge."

Tyler typed back, "But my plants always get bigger anyway. They're growing no matter what." He stared at the little green sprouts, touching a leaf with one finger, cool and slightly fuzzy. If he dumped Blast on both pots and both plants shot up, what would that prove? Nothing, really. Maybe they would have shot up anyway. He needed to see what happened to a plant that got everything except the Blast.

He set up two identical pots on the kitchen windowsill, same soil from the same bag, same amount of water from the same measuring cup, same sunlight through the same glass. Pot A got the Blast mixed into its water. Pot B got plain water and nothing else. He posted a photo of both pots in the chat. Aiden asked, "Why did you do two?" Tyler wrote, "It's called a control group. It gets everything the test pot gets except the one thing being tested. So if Pot A ends up different, I'll know it was the Blast." Ms. Zhou, whose name he'd added after she agreed to supervise his fair project over messages, replied with a single thumbs up, which felt like a standing ovation.

The deadline gnawed at him all week. Six days left, and the two plants looked exactly the same, and his poster board was blank. On Wednesday, Dakota sent the video guy's follow-up post, where he admitted his one testimonial was his own single plant on a south-facing porch. "That's a story about one person's plant," Tyler typed, chewing his thumbnail. "It's not evidence. One plant could be huge for any reason." Dakota wrote, "So the guy in the video is basically my anonymous plant." "Basically," Aiden said.

By Sunday night, both plants had grown, but Pot A stood a thumb-width taller and had two extra leaves. Tyler measured the height of each three times and worked out the ratio, Pot A to Pot B, and wrote it on a sticky note in black marker: 1.4 to 1. Not doubled, like the video claimed. Something real, though, and something he could point to. He messaged the chat, "Small difference. But a real one, because Pot B is the proof of what happens without it."

At 10:52 that night he taped the last photo onto the poster, the two pots side by side in the window, morning light slanting across the labels he had written in careful block letters: TEST and CONTROL. His mom leaned in the doorway and said, "Which one's which?" Tyler pointed at the smaller plant. "That one," he said. "That one's the whole experiment."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
George had been fighting the violin for three weeks, and the violin was winning. Every Saturday he sat in Ms. Costa's studio, a small room above the hardware store that smelled of rosin and old carpet, and every Saturday the E string laughed at him.

The trouble was tuning. Ms. Costa could tighten or loosen a peg and land exactly on the note she wanted, but when George tried it, the string went sharp or flat in wild leaps. Today, though, he had a plan. He had noticed something last week, when Rosalyn, who took the lesson before his, had loosened her peg while plucking the string. Each time she turned the peg, the note slid lower. That had to mean something.

He plucked the E string and listened. Then he turned the peg a tiny amount, plucked again, and the pitch dropped. He turned it back the other way, and the pitch climbed. He did it four more times, marking each movement with his finger on the peg, and there it was, plain as a footprint: turning the peg one way made the string vibrate slower, and the note went lower; turning it the other way made it vibrate faster, and the note went higher. The string itself was telling on itself.

"Ms. Costa," he said, "I think I've been turning the peg too far every time. The note changes more than I expect."

Ms. Costa looked up from the music she was marking. "Show me."

He plucked, turned the peg a whisker, plucked again. The note sank just below where it belonged. He nudged the peg back, plucked, and it rose home. He matched it to the pitch pipe she kept on the piano, and the two sounds folded together into one.

"Pitch," he said, mostly to himself, "is just how fast the string vibrates. Faster is higher. Slower is lower. It's not a mystery at all."

Rosalyn, waiting on the bench by the window for her ride, leaned forward. "That's how mine kept going flat last week. I was loosening the peg and the note just slid down."

"Exactly," said George. He had thought of the violin as an adversary, something hiding its rules from him, but the rules weren't hidden. You just had to listen for them.

Ms. Costa handed him the A string next, the one he dreaded, and supervised while he worked. George plucked, turned, plucked, and brought the note up out of the murk until it rang clean and molten, bright as poured gold. He tuned the D and the G the same way, slow and patient, and when all four strings agreed at last, he drew the bow across them in one careful stroke.

"Play the scale," said Ms. Costa.

George played it, every note in tune, and Rosalyn clapped twice from the window before his bow finished the last note.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
Harrison had been promised that today's science trip to the pond would involve a microscope, and he had assumed that meant looking at pond water. Instead Ms. Foster set a crate of onions on the picnic table and said something about cell walls, which struck him as a strange thing to bring to a pond.

"Tweezers," she said, and passed them around. "One layer of skin. The thinnest you can manage."

Harrison peeled his onion and pulled off a scrap of skin so thin it was almost invisible, like a scrap of wet plastic wrap. Under the little field microscope it turned into a patchwork of brick shapes, each one edged in a darker line. Julian, working the microscope beside him, was less impressed.

"It says fifty on the lens," Julian announced. "Fifty times. That's barely anything."

"That's the objective," Harrison said, leaning over to look. Stamped around the lens it read 40x. "What does the eyepiece say?"

"Ten. So, fifty total. Fifty times bigger."

Harrison frowned at that. Julian had added the numbers, which seemed reasonable until you thought about it for two seconds. "You don't add them," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "It's the eyepiece times the objective. The eyepiece is magnifying the already-magnified picture. So it's ten times forty."

Julian did the multiplication on the back of his hand with a pencil Mercedes handed over without being asked, as if she had been waiting all morning for exactly this. "Four hundred," he admitted. "That's not fifty at all. Fifty would be equivalent to, what, the objective being five."

"It would be a five times objective with a ten eyepiece," Harrison agreed. "Which nobody has."

Mercedes, who had finished her own slide, was now lying on the grass in a manner she clearly considered leisure but which was mostly an excuse to do nothing while other people argued. "So your cells are four hundred times bigger than real," she said to the sky. "Congratulations. They're still onions."

Ms. Foster came around to check their drawings before the bus retired them all back to school at three o'clock sharp. She looked at Harrison's labeled sketch, where he had marked the dark rim of each brick as the cell wall and the faint inner edge as the membrane. She tapped the small dark dot he had drawn in the middle.

"And this?"

"The nucleus," Harrison said. "I think. It's the only thing in there that looks like it's actually in charge."

She moved on without correcting him, which he decided to take as a win. Julian, meanwhile, had begun turning every dial on his microscope at once, and the two of them watched his onion cells swim, blur, and snap back into focus.

"There it is again," Julian said. "Four hundred times. Still an onion."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: The brain's main reward pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area, deep in the brain, to the nucleus accumbens, and addictive drugs boost dopamine along it.
story:
Max stood at the row of sinks, holding his brain diagram up to the mirror like an actor running lines. The health fair was in forty minutes, and Ms. Chan had said his explanation of nicotine addiction still sounded like he was reading a cereal box. He pointed at the diagram, where a thick arrow ran from a dark patch deep in the middle of the brain toward the front. "Nicotine hits the ventral tegmental area, deep in the brain," he told his reflection, "and the signal travels all the way to the nucleus accumbens. That's the brain's main reward pathway. Addictive drugs boost dopamine along it, way more than normal rewards do."

Willow leaned against the paper towel dispenser, timing him on her phone. "Thirty seconds," she said. "Better. But you illustrated the pathway with your finger like it's a subway map. Try saying why that matters." She wanted the fair over for her own reason: her older sister had promised to quit three times, and Willow had signed up to judge the addiction posters so she could bring the best one home. "Again," she said. "Slower."

Before Max could start, a folded note slid under the far stall door and drifted across the tiles. He picked it up. In shaky handwriting it said, "Don't say my name at the fair. I threw it in the dumpster behind the gym. Not everything, but most. You seem like you actually get this stuff, so explain it right, okay? The part about the pathway. People think it's just weakness. It isn't."

The bathroom went quiet except for a drip from the tap. Max knew that handwriting from every group project since fourth grade. He knocked softly on the stall door. "Brenden?" The lock rattled, the door swung open, and out stepped Brenden, eyes red, holding a plastic device that he must not have thrown away after all. "I couldn't find the dumpster key," Brenden said. "The gate was locked. So it's still in my pocket, and I'm still that guy who lies in notes."

Max looked at his own diagram, at the arrow running deep brain to front, then at his friend. He held out the paper. "Here. Read this part out loud. Ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, dopamine boosted along the whole path. If you understand it, you can explain it better than me, because you've felt it." Brenden stared at the diagram like a man staring at a barren field where a forest should be, then began to read, slowly, under the buzzing canopy of the ceiling lights.

"We'll go on right after you," Willow said, and pulled open the bathroom door to the noise of the fair.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
story:
The kitchen smelled of cardamom and toasted almonds, because his mother was making sweets for the party, and Michael sat at the counter with the pages of Surah Al-Mulk spread out in front of him like a map he kept unfolding. He had to recite it by heart at his coming-of-age ceremony in three weeks. Three weeks. He read the first verse aloud, stumbled, started over, stumbled again, and let his forehead drop onto the paper.

"You sound like a printer that's jamming," said Mannat, who had come over to "help," which so far meant eating almonds. She was doing the same thing for her own ceremony, but her surah was shorter, and she had finished it two days ago and would not stop mentioning it.

Michael remembered then their cousin who had visited last summer, the one who had stood in this same kitchen and recited for nearly an hour without a single page in front of him. Michael had asked him how, and he had said, "I'm a hafiz. A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters." Then he had laughed and added that it never stayed memorized on its own, that keeping it perfectly remembered took constant practice, every single day, like feeding something. At the time Michael had thought that sounded miserable. Now, staring at his fourth failed attempt, he thought about it differently. His cousin had not learned by staring at pages. He had used the kitchen timer, twenty minutes at a time, standing up, reciting out loud, the same small chunk over and over until it was agile on his tongue, then adding the next chunk the next day.

Michael pushed the pages aside and changed his mind about his whole method. He stood up, set the oven timer for ten minutes, and recited only the first four verses, out loud, walking back and forth between the sink and the fridge. The overhead light refracted off the sugar bowl and threw a small rainbow on the counter, and he recited to it as if it were an audience. When the timer beeped, he tried the four verses with his eyes closed. They came out whole.

"Twenty minutes a day," he told Mannat. "Just a piece at a time, every day, even after the ceremony. That's the trick. You don't stop."

Mannat swallowed her almond. "Even after?"

"Even after," Michael said, and closed his eyes and began again, verse five, slow and careful, the timer ticking between them.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
story:
Elijah stood in front of the washing machine holding two shirts, one white and one new red, and tried to remember what his mom had said before she left for the weekend. "Sort the darks from the lights," she had told him, "and don't wash the red one with anything you like." Her text that morning had been more specific: "Darks together, cold water, and don't overload it. Love you. P.S. there's pizza money on the counter." He had read it three times, but it had said nothing about the orange stain spreading across the front of Kyan's grey hoodie, which Elijah had borrowed Friday night and spilled pizza grease on at Annalise's birthday party.

He remembered the party in a flash: the slice folding in his hand, the grease landing dead centre on the chest, Kyan laughing so hard he knocked over his own cup. Kyan had said it was fine, but Kyan said everything was fine. Elijah had run the hoodie under the tap the moment he got home, scrubbing it with his thumbs until his knuckles ached, and the stain had not faded even a little. That gave him his first premise: water alone was not going to do it. Something invisible had to be holding the grease onto the fabric, and plain water couldn't grab whatever it was.

He turned the detergent bottle over and read the back, where it talked about grease. Annalise had said something once in science about detergent, something about how it worked on both oil and water at once. He squinted at the label and tried to interpret what it meant. Then he thought he saw it. Detergent molecules had one end that grabbed water and another end that grabbed oil and grease, so they could lift greasy dirt off the fabric and drag it into the wash water. If that was true, then the stain wasn't stuck forever. It was just waiting for something that could hold onto both at once.

He rubbed a drop of liquid detergent straight into the orange spot, worked it in with his fingers, and dropped the hoodie in with the darks on cold. While the machine churned, he scrubbed the counter, folded the towels from the dryer badly, then better, and texted Annalise: "-testing a theory on Kyan's hoodie. If it works I'm basically a scientist." She sent back a thumbs-up and "chronic overthinker but go off."

When he pulled the hoodie out, the stain was gone. Elijah stared at the clean grey fabric, then folded it into a neat square, the way his mom folded his, and set it by the door. Then he noticed the hoodie's inside tag, which he had never read: it said a name, but not Kyan's. He snapped a photo and sent it to Kyan. "Whose hoodie is this actually?" The reply came fast. "annalise's. she left it at my place in september. you GREASED it??"

Elijah looked at the folded square, then at his phone, and typed, "I have never been happier to say it's clean."

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: A two-column proof lists each statement in the left column and the reason it is true, such as a given fact or a rule, in the right column.
story:
Elena slid into her seat at the tutoring centre just as Ms. Bautista flipped the timer to fifteen minutes. On the whiteboard were two triangles, and below them a proof split into two tall columns.

"Side-angle-side," Alec whispered across the table. "The one where two sides and the angle between them match up. If we get the reasons column filled before the timer, we win the last slice of Melia's birthday cake."

Elena read the board fast. "Look, the statements are all in the left column," she said, tapping the paper in front of her. "So every line in the right column has to say why that statement is true." She copied the setup onto her own sheet, statements on the left, blank reasons on the right, and felt her pencil hovering over the first empty box.

Melia leaned over. "I can speculate all day about why line two is true, but we should just agree and write it."

"Line one is given," Elena said. "It literally says 'given' right there in the problem. And line two, the sides are equal because that's the tick marks on the diagram, so the reason is, what, 'given' too? Or is there a rule name?"

Alec flipped through his notes so fast the pages flapped. "Wait, wait. Ms. Bautista said a reason can be a given fact or a rule. So the tick marks are a given, and the angle in the middle, that's where the rule kicks in." He wrote "given" beside line two before anyone could argue.

Elena stared at the third statement, the one claiming the big triangles were congruent. "That's our rule," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Two sides and the angle squeezed between them, and the whole thing follows from side-angle-side." She printed SAS beside the statement, then double-checked the diagram to make sure the marked angle really sat between the marked sides, not just near them. It did. The pattern held.

"Consensus?" Melia asked, holding up her sheet. All three papers matched, reasons lined up beside statements all the way down.

"Ten seconds," Ms. Bautista called out.

Alec raised his hand so high his chair tipped. Ms. Bautista walked over, ran her pen down the right column, and nodded. "Eloquent work," she said, "clean reasons, every one earned." She sliced the cake into three pieces and handed Elena the fork first.

Elena took a bite, still grinning at the board. "Next time," she said, "I want the statement column too."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
story:
Chloe sat at the kitchen table with a box of tissues, a mug of warm water, and her math homework, which she had no intention of touching. This was her third cold since fall, and she had decided that was too many. Nihal had already texted her the class notes twice, and Aaryan had texted a drawing of a microbe wearing a scarf, which was supposed to be funny. Chloe coughed and pulled a notebook toward her instead of the homework.

At the top of the page she wrote "COLD COUNT." She made a column for herself and put three tally marks in it, one for each cold since September. Then she made columns for her mother, her father, and her little brother, who was at school and, as far as she knew, healthy. She texted Nihal: how many colds have you had since fall? Nihal wrote back "three, why?" Aaryan wrote "two." She added two more columns and tallied those. Her reasoning went like this: if she could count colds for enough people, she could figure out whether three was actually strange or just normal, and whether there was a pattern, like little kids catching more than big ones.

Her mother came through the kitchen in an elastic headband, pulling her hair back before starting dinner. She had her phone in her hand. "Ms. Saleh from next door dropped soup on the porch," her mother said. "She says feel better." Chloe asked her the counting question straight out: how many colds since fall, for you, for Dad, for her brother? Her mother said one for herself, two for Dad, and she'd have to think about the little one. Then she added, "I read something at the clinic, actually. It said adults average two to three colds a year, and children often catch more than that." She said it while chopping an onion, not like a lesson, just like a fact she'd happened to read.

Chloe stared at her tally chart. Three colds for herself, three for Nihal, two for Aaryan, two for her dad, one for her mother. The adults weren't above the average. The kids were at or above two already, and it was only January. She had been operating on a hidden assumption, that she was somehow catching colds wrong, and now the numbers didn't support it. But she wanted one more data point, so she wrote her brother's name at the bottom of the chart and decided to wait.

When he got off the bus that afternoon, Chloe was waiting in the kitchen with the notebook and a pen. "Have you had a cold since September? A real one, not a sniffle," she said. He said he'd had one in October, and then there was the week before Thanksgiving when he'd stayed home two days. She drew a second tally mark next to his name, slowly, to make it official. Then she tore out a fresh page and wrote "JANUARY" at the top. "You're going in the chart," she told him. "Everybody in this family is going in the chart."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats.
story:
Cameron had been begging for a dog since second grade, and on Saturday morning his wish finally arrived in a cardboard box lined with an old towel. The puppy was brown and white with one ear that flopped the wrong way, and his dad said Cameron would be the one to supervise her feeding, walking, and training, every single day. Cameron named her Biscuit before the box was even unpacked.

That afternoon, Madelyn came over to meet the new dog, and she brought a bag of trail mix to share while they watched Biscuit explore the living room. Biscuit sniffed the couch, the coffee table, and then Madelyn's shoelaces, and when Cameron popped a few raisins into his mouth, Biscuit sat down in front of him and stared with big hopeful eyes. Cameron held one out toward her, because that was what you did with a dog who looked that hungry, wasn't it?

"Stop!" Madelyn grabbed his wrist. "Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats. Not even one."

Cameron pulled his hand back and stared at the little wrinkled raisin in his fingers. It seemed impossible that something so small and ordinary could hurt anybody. But then he started thinking about it like the problems Ms. Mercer gave them in science, where you had to figure out the hidden rule from what you observed. He couldn't see inside Biscuit's body, and he couldn't ask her how she felt, so how could he test whether Madelyn was right?

He didn't test it on Biscuit, because that was the one thing the rule said never to do. Instead he looked it up on his dad's phone, and every answer said the same thing in different words, which was how you knew something was probably true rather than one person's guess. Then he did what he thought a real scientist would do: he emptied the trail mix into a jar, wrote "NOT FOR DOGS" on a sticky note, and put the jar on the highest shelf in the pantry. Biscuit watched the whole operation from the floor, tail wagging, completely unbothered.

"Sorry, girl," Cameron said. "You can have dog treats instead."

Later they played courtroom, the way they did in class when Ms. Mercer assigned mock trials. Biscuit was the defendant, accused of chewing Dad's slipper, and Cameron argued that a dog who had only been home for six hours deserved a second chance. Madelyn was the judge, and she ruled that the defendant was guilty but cute, which carried a sentence of one more hour of playing in the backyard.

After Madelyn went home, Cameron sat on the porch steps with Biscuit's head warm against his knee, and made a list titled "Biscuit Rules." At the top, in his best handwriting, he wrote: no grapes, no raisins, ever. Biscuit licked the corner of the notebook, leaving a small wet spot right beside the words.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
The morning Anna's family pulled into Seaside National Park, she could hardly sit still. The plan was to meet their neighbour Ms. Virtanen and her grandkids, Lyna and Jaiveer, right at the beach by the dunes. Anna had been counting down for two weeks. She grabbed her towel before the car fully stopped.

The water was choppier than it looked in the park brochure. A yellow sign stood at the top of the sand, and Jaiveer jogged over to read it. "It says watch for rip currents," he called. "What are you supposed to do if the water pulls you out?" Anna squinted at the sign. She flashed back to last summer at the community pool, when she'd read a safety poster while waiting for swim lessons. The poster had a picture of a swimmer moving sideways, along the shore, not toward it. She remembered the exact words: swim parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, instead of straight against it. "You don't fight it head on," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "You go sideways until you're out of it." Lyna looked skeptical. "Sideways? That feels like giving up." She'd always believed the strongest swimmer should just power straight back in.

The three of them asked Ms. Virtanen if they could swim out to the sandbar, and she compromised: they could go in past the breakers only if they stayed together and came back at her whistle. The waves were cold and thrilling. Then Anna noticed something odd. A line of foamy, churning water stretched from the sandbar toward open sea, narrow, like a river inside the ocean, while the water on either side of it sat calm. A rip current. She couldn't see the current itself, only its footprint on the surface, and that was enough to make her chest tighten.

Before she could call out, Jaiveer, floating nearby, gave a yelp and began drifting out along that foamy line, kicking hard toward the beach and getting nowhere. "Don't swim straight against it!" Anna shouted, her voice cracking. "Go sideways, along the beach!" Lyna, who had changed her mind about the whole sideways business the instant she saw Jaiveer slipping, cupped her hands and yelled it too. "Parallel! Move parallel!" Jaiveer turned, swam along the shore, and after a few strokes the grip of the water simply let go of him. He angled in through the calm water and stumbled onto the sand, breathless and grinning.

Ms. Virtanen wrapped a towel around him, and from her perspective the whole thing had lasted less than a minute, though to Anna it had felt long and sinister and enormous. "That sign is coming home in my memory," Jaiveer announced. "Next time I'm the one who gets to explain it." Anna laughed and pointed at the water, where the narrow line of foam still streamed seaward, patient and quiet. "First one to spot the next one wins," she said.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
story:
Cameron sat on Nicholas's bedroom floor with Rhys, staring at the laptop screen between them. A sleek website promised that VivoSlim, a green powder you stirred into water, would "flush toxins from the intestine in nine days." Nicholas had already filled in his mom's credit card information and was one click away from spending forty dollars.

"Wait," Cameron said. "Don't click it yet."

"Why not? Look at it. Doctors in white coats, testimonials, a lab photo." Nicholas turned the laptop so Cameron could evaluate the site himself. It did look convincing. There was a whole page of five-star reviews and a section called "The Science."

Rhys leaned over Cameron's shoulder. "My cousin bought something like this once. It did nothing."

"That's just her opinion," Nicholas said. "This site is full of proof."

Cameron frowned. Rhys's cousin doing nothing wasn't proof either way, it was one story. But the website's own pages weren't proof either. The site was run by people selling the powder, so of course it said the powder was amazing. He needed something the sellers didn't control. "Can I open some new tabs?" he asked, and before Nicholas could answer, he was typing.

He searched for the company that made VivoSlim. The first result was a news article about the company being fined for false advertising two years earlier. The second was a forum where people complained the powder was just expensive fiber. The third was a government consumer page listing the company among businesses with repeated complaints. Cameron felt his heartbeat pick up. It was like judging a stranger: instead of listening to the stranger describe himself, you asked the neighbors.

"Look at this," he said, spreading the three tabs across the screen.

Nicholas read them in silence. "So the site says one thing, and everything outside the site says the opposite."

"Exactly." Cameron had read about this once in a library book about how professional fact-checkers work. "They call it lateral reading. You don't stay on the website judging it. You open new tabs and see what other sources say about it."

Rhys grinned. "Tab army."

Nicholas deleted the credit card number slowly, like he was deflating. "I really wanted it to work. Coach says I need to get stronger for spring season."

"Getting stronger takes actual food and actual practice," Rhys said. "Aggressive amounts of peanut butter. My cousin swears by it."

Nicholas laughed, and Cameron started a new search, fingers already moving. "Let's look up protein stuff for athletes. Same method."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A desert is often defined as a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters, or 10 inches, of rain a year.
story:
The trail climbed through pinyon pines, and Alexa's graph flapped in the breeze as she walked. Mr. Rodríguez had said their climate comparisons were due at the start of class tomorrow, and hers still had a hole in it.

"Look at this," she said, catching up to Hadley and Sehaj at a switchback. She held out two printed graphs. One showed a rainforest in Brazil, with monthly rainfall bars stacked so tall they looked like green towers. The other showed the Sonoran Desert, where the bars barely rose off the bottom line. "Rainforest gets over two thousand millimeters a year. The desert gets, like, two hundred."

"So the desert's the dry one, the rainforest's the wet one. Done," Hadley said. "Can we eat lunch now?"

"No, not done." Alexa stopped on a flat slab of rock. "I found this other graph last night. Antarctica. And it's snowy and freezing, but the rainfall part, the precipitation, is super low. Lower than this desert." She frowned at the paper. "So is a desert about heat, or about rain? Because those are two different things. Temperature is one factor and rainfall is another factor, and my poster treats them like the same thing."

Sehaj leaned over her shoulder. "What does the textbook say a desert is?"

"That's the problem. It says a desert is a place that gets less than about two hundred fifty millimeters of rain a year." She traced the line on her desert graph with one finger. "Ten inches. This place is under it. And so is..."

She stopped. The sun hit the rocks around them, making them look almost molten where the light pooled in the hollows. Somewhere below, water dripped from a seep into a dark tinaja, drop by slow drop.

"Antarctica," she said. "Antarctica counts. A cold, snowy place can be a desert."

Hadley laughed. "No way. That can't be right."

"Check the number," Sehaj said, pulling out his phone. He found the rainfall chart for an Antarctic station and held it up beside Alexa's desert graph. The bars on both of them hugged the bottom of the page.

Alexa pulled her pencil from her pack and, right there on the rock, drew a new vertical line on her poster draft. One side: deserts, defined by rainfall. The other side: hot and cold, defined by temperature. "The graph can convey both at once," she said, mostly to herself. "Rainfall bars decide if it's a desert. Temperature line decides if it's hot or cold. Two separate questions."

They hiked the last mile fast, Alexa sketching as she walked, Hadley steadying her elbow on the steep parts so she wouldn't pitch off the trail. At the trailhead Mr. Rodríguez was waiting by the vans, checking his watch.

"Cutting it close," he said.

She held up the poster, crosshatched with pencil lines. "Mr. Rodríguez, is it true a cold, snowy place counts as a desert?"

He looked at the graph, then at her. "If it gets less than about two hundred fifty millimeters of rain a year, ten inches, then yes. Rainfall decides it."

Alexa grinned and turned the poster toward Hadley. "Told you."

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: Shakespeare wrote much of his verse in iambic pentameter: lines of about ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
story:
Emile sat at the kitchen table with the biggest book he had ever been assigned, open to a speech from A Midsummer Night's Dream. His homework, written on the board by Mr. Wanjiru, was to paraphrase the speech into modern English, and so far he had written one sentence and crossed it out twice. "I know each word," he muttered, "but I don't know what the sentence is doing."

He texted his classmate Douglas. "How do you even start this?"

"Tap it," Douglas wrote back. "You know. Like in class."

Emile leaned back and let himself remember Tuesday. Mr. Wanjiru had walked in, said "desks, please," and started everyone drumming their fingers in a steady beat, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, five times per line. Then he read the speech aloud over the drumming, and the words had landed on the beats like feet on stairs. Onyx, who sat behind Emile, had whispered, "It's called iambic pentameter," and Emile had thought it was a weird name for something that sounded so much like a heartbeat.

Back at his kitchen table, he put his hand flat on the wood and tried it. He read the first line slowly: "Thou art as wise as thou art beautiful." He tapped as he read, and the syllables fell into place, ten of them, five soft-then-strong pairs, the beat rising on art, wise, thou, and the last part of beautiful. When he lost count on line three, he tapped again and found he had swallowed a syllable, saying "e'en" as "even." The rhythm had caught him. It was like a metal detector for words he was skipping.

"So the important words are the loud ones," he said out loud. He underlined the stressed words in pencil, and a paraphrase came almost by itself: "You're just as smart as you are good-looking." It sounded like something Douglas would say to Onyx after a test.

Then came the twist. On the last line, he tapped da-DUM five times and the syllables refused to comply, sliding off the beat no matter how he read it. He counted the syllables with his pencil point. Eleven, and the stresses landed crooked. He read it again, and again, and finally laughed. Not every line obeyed the pattern, and that was fine, because the meaning was still clear once he stopped forcing it. He wrote his paraphrase, checked his citation of act and scene at the bottom of the page, and closed the book.

The kitchen smelled like the pasta his dad was cooking. Emile carried his paper over and read the paraphrase aloud, tapping the counter with two fingers, da-DUM, da-DUM, all the way to the end.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, including weekends, helps keep the body's internal clock, called the circadian rhythm, steady.
story:
Ethan kept losing the ball. It was the third Tuesday in a row that he'd fumbled a pass in gym class, and Gabriel had noticed. "You look like you didn't sleep for a week," Gabriel said as they walked to the locker room. Ethan shrugged, but he knew the truth: he had slept, just badly, and only on some nights. He couldn't quite articulate what was wrong, except that Monday mornings felt like wading through glue while everyone else jogged past him.

Mr. Huang, who ran the after-school chess club, watched Ethan stare at the board without moving a piece. "You're holding your breath," Mr. Huang said quietly. Ethan blinked. He was. Mr. Huang tapped his own chest. "Try slow breaths. In for four, out for four. It's free, and nobody has to know you're doing it." Ethan tried it, and to his surprise, his thoughts stopped tumbling long enough for him to spot a move he'd been missing. Interesting, he thought. His body had been sending signals, and he'd been ignoring all of them.

That night he started a list in his notebook. Monday, terrible. Tuesday, bad. Then he noticed something odd: Saturday and Sunday were circled with a sloppy star, because he slept until noon both days and felt great. So why did Monday feel like the worst day of his life? He flipped back through two weeks of notes. The pattern was so obvious he almost laughed. Good weekend sleep, terrible Monday. No weekend sleep routine, terrible everything. Could the problem be the thing that felt best?

He asked Bennett in the cafeteria, sketching the ratio on a napkin: two good weekend days versus three terrible school days. "What if sleeping in is the cause?" Bennett said. "That doesn't even make sense." "It might," Ethan said. He'd found a word in the library that afternoon while looking it up: circadian rhythm. "It's the body's internal clock," he told Bennett, "and keeping a steady bedtime and wake time, even on weekends, keeps it steady." Bennett looked skeptical.
