"So you're going to get up at six thirty on Saturday. Voluntarily."

The first weekend was brutal. His alarm went off, the sun wasn't up, and no part of him felt immune to the misery of it. He did his four-count breathing lying in bed, which at least stopped him from throwing the alarm across the room. By Saturday afternoon, though, he noticed he wasn't dragging. Sunday felt the same. And Monday morning, when the alarm sounded, his eyes actually opened before it rang.

In gym class on Tuesday, Gabriel threw him the ball in a tight spiral. Ethan caught it without thinking, pivoted, and passed it back clean. "There he is," Gabriel said. Ethan grinned and took one slow breath, in for four, out for four, just because he could.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
story:
Norah stood at the canoe launch with her duffel bag balanced on one shoulder, watching the aluminum boats knock gently against the dock. Tomorrow the camp bus would take her north for a whole month, and her mother had signed her up for the paddling clinic this afternoon so she would not arrive at camp as the only girl who had never sat in a canoe. The problem was that Norah had never sat in a canoe, and the water looked deeper than it probably was.

"Just step in," said Bentley, who was already settled on the dock with a bag of chips. "It's a boat. How hard can it be?"

Norah noticed that Mr. Krause, the man running the clinic, kept his knees bent and his pack low when he loaded gear, and she wondered whether that mattered. She grabbed the gunwale, the edge of the canoe, and put one foot right on the side. The whole boat tipped toward the water so fast that she yelped and let go.

"You nearly demonstrated how to fall in," Bentley said, laughing.

Avah arrived late, life jacket half buckled, and climbed in after Norah without any trouble at all. Norah watched her do it. Avah had stepped into the middle of the boat, low and crouched, and the canoe had barely swayed. Was it the person, or the spot? Norah decided to test it. She got out, then stepped back in again, this time placing her foot on the center line of the hull and dropping to her knees right away. The canoe held steady, solid as a picnic table. When she tried shifting her weight to one side, it wobbled at once. So that was the rule, she thought: keep your weight low and centered, and the canoe stays calm. No wonder people always step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.

"See, you have the constitution of a river guide," Mr. Krause called from the next boat over. "Most beginners tip twice before they learn that."

Out on the water, Avah paddled in the bow while Norah steered from the stern. A first-timer named Danny in a bright orange life jacket passed them going the other way, wobbling wildly, and Norah could guess exactly why before he even spoke.

"I stepped on the edge and it almost threw me," Danny called. "Why does it do that?"

Norah grinned and turned her paddle flat in the water, slowing them side by side. "Watch," she said, and she shifted her knees an inch off the center line. The canoe rocked. She slid back to the middle and it steadied like magic. "Weight low and centered. That's the whole secret. Want to try it?"

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
The group chat lit up at 4:32 on Thursday, right after track practice. Emerald sent a photo of a green bottle with a lightning bolt on it, captioned, "Volt Rush. Drank it before the 400 and took two whole seconds off my time. Buying a case."

Avery stared at her phone. Two seconds was a lot. But she kept thinking about last month, when Emerald had sworn a lucky hair tie made her clears higher, and then lost the tie and cleared the same height anyway. "How much was that bottle?" Avery typed. "Five dollars," Emerald answered, followed by three flexing emojis. Mariam wrote, "Where do I get one?" That gave Avery an ominous feeling, like watching everyone line up to hand over their allowance for nothing she could prove existed. She typed, "Meet me at the track tomorrow, 10 a.m. Bring the bottle. I have an idea."

Friday morning, Avery filled an empty Volt Rush bottle with water from her kitchen tap. The technique felt sneaky, and she remembered the time in fourth grade when she'd swapped her dad's coffee for decaf as a joke and he'd claimed it was "the best cup all week" until she told him. He had laughed. She hoped Emerald would too. At the track, Emerald chugged the "drink," stretched, and Avery clicked the stopwatch. 61.4 seconds, four tenths faster than Thursday.

"Okay," Avery said, holding up the real bottle, which was full of water. Emerald froze mid-victory-dance. "You mean I just PR'd on water?" Avery nodded. "I think the believing did the work. When you expect something to help, it can make you feel better or faster even if there's nothing active in it. Mr. Kamau said that once, in science. He called it the placebo effect." Mariam, who had come to watch, groaned. "So my five dollars is still in my pocket. Good."

Emerald sat on the infield grass for a while, turning the empty bottle in her hands. Then she stood, brushed off her shorts, and set the bottle on the fence post. "Race you to the bleachers," she said. "No bottle. Winner summarizes the plan for Saturday."

Avery sprinted after her, the stopwatch bouncing in her pocket.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
story:
Ella pressed her eye against the microscope until her lashes touched the glass, and still the onion skin looked like nothing but pale bricks. Tenley, on the next stool, had already finished her drawing and was labeling her cell wall with neat little arrows.

"Try the fine focus," Tenley said. "Tiny turns. Don't be so obstinate about it."

"I'm not obstinate," Ella said, turning the knob in the smallest movement she could manage. Last year she had refused to ask for help on the fractions unit until she was three worksheets behind, and she had promised herself she would stop doing that. She turned the knob again, and suddenly the bricks sharpened into bordered boxes, each one wrapped in its own dark outline. Inside one of them sat a small dense dot, like a fingerprint pressed into wet clay.

"There it is," she said. "The nucleus." She started her drawing, then stopped with her pencil hovering. "Who even figured out that dot was there? Somebody had to be the first person to look and think it mattered."

Tenley shrugged, but Kaleigh leaned over from the water-fountain line. "We had that last period. The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831, while he was studying orchid cells."

"Orchids," Ella repeated. She looked back into the eyepiece. Not onions, orchids. Somebody two hundred years ago had squinted at a different plant, seen the same stubborn dot she was staring at right now, and decided it deserved a name. She wrote "nucleus" beside her drawing, then hesitated over the wall and the membrane, which were lying so close together she could not tell where one ended and the other began.

She decided to test it. "Mr. Rivera, if I focus down through the edge of the cell, can I see the wall and the membrane separately?"

"Try it and tell me," he said, which was his answer to almost everything.

Ella found a cell at the torn edge of the skin, where the layers peeled apart like the skin of a bubble. She focused slowly downward. The thick outer line stayed put; the thinner inner one wrinkled and shifted, following the inside edge like a second skin. Wall outside, membrane inside. She labeled both, and only then did she notice she had drawn the nucleus in every single cell on her page, because every cell on the slide had one. Not maybe. Every one.

By the window, Kaleigh was reading a poster about Louis Pasteur for her own lab sheet. "He proved a microbe could make milk go bad," she said, mostly to herself. "One invisible thing, whole big effect."

Ella thought about that on the bus home, cheek against the cold window. She had almost not turned the fine focus knob. She had almost decided the slide was blank and waited for Tenley's answers, the way she used to, and she would never have seen the dot at all. She still wasn't sure whether she was brave or just stubborn, and she turned the word "obstinate" over in her mind until it lost its shape.

At home she set her lab sheet on the kitchen table. Her mom glanced at the drawing of brick-shaped cells. "You're going to invest in a microscope of your own next, aren't you?"

"Maybe," Ella said. She picked up her pencil and added one more label at the bottom, small enough that only she would read it: "Brown, orchids, 1831."

Then she went to find a book about orchids.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a flat horizontal line means the object is not moving.
story:
The gym hallway had a long stretch of tile floor, and Aurora had claimed it with a roll of masking tape and a meter stick. Selma stood at the far end holding the stopwatch like it might go off in her hand.

"Other group got a ball across the whole hall in four seconds," Selma said. "We're going to beat that. Ready?"

Aurora set the marble at the top of the ramp they'd built from a binder propped on a stack of dictionaries. The table wobbled when she let go, so first she folded a napkin and wedged it under the short leg until the whole thing felt stable. Then she rolled. Selma called out the times at each meter mark, and Aurora wrote them in her table, one column for distance, one for time, the numbers marching along in a neat diagonal.

Back in the science room, Ms. Adebayo let the worksheets circulate while everyone started their graphs. Aurora plotted her points, drew the line, and then stopped. Between two seconds and four seconds, her line went flat. Perfectly flat. She checked her table twice. The distance numbers for those rows were identical.

Selma leaned over. "That's wrong. The ball was going fast, you said."

"It went fast, then something happened, then fast again," Aurora said slowly. She looked at the flat stretch. Somewhere in the middle of that line, the ball had stopped covering distance. She thought about the hallway: the ramp, the tile, the strip of carpet by the doors, the tile again.

"The carpet," she said. "It got stuck on the carpet. Look, distance doesn't change there. A flat line means it isn't moving."

Selma frowned at the paper. "So our graph says our fast ball took a nap in the middle of the run."

Aurora laughed, which was a mistake, because it caught the attention of Romie, whose graph was on the desk behind them. Romie scooted over with a note already half-written and slid it across.

"It's flat too," the note said. "Mine flatlines from one second to five seconds. Our ball never got past the spot where somebody's backpack was sitting. Is my graph broken or is this a thing?"

Aurora wrote back underneath. "It's a thing. Draw an arrow to the flat part and label it stuck. Then look at your data and tell me what was in the way."

On the wall above the sinks, a poster from the last unit showed a diagram of an intestine, coiled like a garden hose, with arrows tracing its path. Aurora glanced at it and decided her graph was more satisfying. A garden hose you could actually read.

At the end of class, Selma was still not satisfied either, but for different reasons. "We never beat four seconds," she said, packing up. "Our ball spent two whole seconds sitting on carpet."

"Then tomorrow we aim the ramp so it misses the carpet," Aurora said. She tore the graph out of her notebook, folded it once, and put it in her pocket with the napkin still stuck to the corner.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Two climate graphs can only be compared by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale; otherwise a short bar may stand for more rain.
story:
Audrey slapped two printed graphs on the library table, one for Cairo and one for Singapore, and announced that today she would finally classify each city's climate before the science fair on Friday. "Easy," said Coen, poking the Singapore sheet. "Singapore wins. Its bars are way taller." Axl leaned over from the next seat, where he was supposedly studying, and squinted at the page. "Taller bars, more rain. That's just math." Audrey frowned. Something about the two pages itched at her, the way a sock seam itches inside a shoe.

"Wait," she said, and pulled both graphs closer. Along the side of Cairo's graph, the rainfall axis climbed in steps of five millimetres. On Singapore's graph, the steps jumped by fifty. She checked twice, because Coen was already doing a victory lap around the table in his chair, which had wheels, which was a mistake. "Coen. Look at the numbers on the sides." He rolled back, looked, and his victory face went sideways. Singapore's tallest bar stopped at two hundred millimetres for its wettest month. Cairo's tallest bar, short and stubby as an eraser, stood for twenty-five. "Huh," Coen said. "The short bar is more rain. That feels illegal." Audrey grinned. "Two graphs only match up by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale. Otherwise a short bar might stand for more rain."

Ms. He drifted past their table on her way to the printer and raised an eyebrow at Coen's chair, which was now parked on top of Axl's foot. "Save the victory laps for after the fair," she said, and kept walking. Audrey wrote the rule in her notebook in big letters, then underlined it twice, then, feeling a small sting of guilt about how smug she'd been about figuring it out first, added a smiley face for Coen's benefit.

That night she got a message from Coen on the class chat app. "Dear Graph Detective," he'd typed, "Axl says the Amazon is fertile because of all that rain, and I said obviously, and then he asked me how much rain, in numbers, and I panicked and said 'lots.' Please send numbers so I can classify the rainforest properly and impress my partner, who is me." Audrey laughed so hard her dad asked what was wrong with her. She wrote back: "Dear Panicked Partner, more than 2,000 mm a year in some places. That's rain bars taller than your chair. Bring snacks tomorrow."

On Friday their poster showed the two graphs side by side, redrawn with matching scales so every bar could be compared fairly. Axl stood beside it wearing a name tag that said RAINFOREST EXPERT, which nobody had asked him to do. A judge stopped, traced the bars with one finger, and nodded. Coen whispered, "If she asks about the axis, you talk." Audrey elbowed him and pointed at the tallest bar on the wall. "Look at that beauty," she said. "Two hundred millimetres in one month."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.
story:
James had wanted a dog for exactly three years, which was how long it had taken his mother to say yes. On Saturday morning they walked into the Riverside Animal Shelter together, and the smell hit him first, disinfectant and kibble, with a hint of wet towel. Behind the front desk, a man with reading glasses looked up from a clipboard.

"I'm Mr. Nwosu," the man said. "You the family adopting today?" James nodded so fast his neck hurt. They followed him past rows of kennels, and one brindle mutt with crooked ears stood up and pressed her whole face against the bars, tail going like a windshield wiper. Her card said Pickles, age about one.

At the meet-and-greet pen, Dalia and Wren were already there waiting, since James had texted them from the car. Pickles nosed Wren's shoelaces, then sat down on James's foot and leaned. "She picked you," Dalia said. "It's objective. Look at the data." She pointed at the dog's weight, warm and heavy on his sneaker. Mr. Nwosu laughed and said the paperwork would take twenty minutes, so James dumped his backpack on a bench to fish out the treats he'd brought, and a strip of sugar-free gum slid out and rolled under the bench. He grabbed it and shoved it back in the front pocket, planning to chew it on the drive home.

Pickles slept the whole way home with her head on James's knee. That evening, in his room, he heard a soft tearing sound and found Pickles under his desk with the backpack, the gum packet open and shredded, most of the pieces gone. His stomach dropped. He tried to remember whether the vet's after-hours number was on the adoption papers, and it was, so he called while his mother held the dog steady. "She ate sugar-free gum," he said when the nurse answered. "Maybe six pieces."

"Read me the ingredients," the nurse said. James squinted at the flattened wrapper in the porch light. "Sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol." The nurse's voice stayed level. "The xylitol is the one we worry about. It makes a dog's body release insulin, and that can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar. Bring her in now."

At the clinic they took Pickles through a door with a round window, and a technician clipped a small sensor to her collar that would track her glucose. James sat in the waiting room between his mother and Dalia, who had biked over. "How did you even know to call?" Dalia asked. "I didn't know," James said. "I just thought, gum is sweet, sweet stuff is fake now, and dogs aren't people. It could be anything in there." He kept his eyes on the round window, where he could see a tail, then not, then the tail again.

The vet came out after an hour. "She threw most of it up, and her numbers look fine. She'll be sleepy tonight and perfectly ordinary by morning." James's mother exhaled loudly. When they brought Pickles out, she walked to James, put her chin on his knee, and yawned so wide he could count her teeth. The next morning he taped a sign inside the front door that read CHECK POCKETS, and on his way to school he nominated Pickles for the shelter's photo wall by emailing Mr. Nwosu the picture Dalia had taken, the one with the dog sitting on his foot. "Send two," Mr. Nwosu wrote back. "One for the wall, one for the fridge."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
Ms. Ahmed had taped old posters above the whiteboard, and Peyton kept staring at one from a 1950s cereal box: "Join the millions who already switched!" Under the hum of the radiator, she copied the slogan into her notebook and added a question mark after it. Millions of what? Switched to what? The poster didn't say a single thing the cereal actually did.

"Ms. Ahmed said these posters used persuasion tricks," Julian whispered from the next desk. "That one looks like the trickiest."

Peyton leaned over. "What does the cereal do better than the old kind?"

Julian squinted at the faded print. "No idea. It just says millions switched."

"So the reason to buy it is... that other people bought it?" Peyton tapped her pencil. What if the millions weren't even real? The poster gave no reason at all, just a crowd. She raised her hand. "Ms. Ahmed, is there a name for when an ad says everyone's doing something instead of saying why it's good?"

"That's called the bandwagon technique," Ms. Ahmed said, and moved on to the next poster.

Bandwagon. Peyton wrote the word down and circled it. The name itself was a clue, like jumping on a wagon because everyone else already climbed aboard. Being left behind must be the fear, she thought, not the cereal. Maybe that was the whole trick: you wanted to belong, so you never stopped to ask what the product did.

At lunch she ran a test. She found an ad in a magazine for a phone that a famous singer supposedly used, with big glowing words like "revolutionary" and "unbeatable," and showed it to Alessio without the product description. "Would you want this?"

"Obviously," Alessio said. "If she uses it, and everyone has it, it must be good."

"Okay, now read this part." Peyton covered the celebrity's picture and the slogan and pointed to the tiny specifications. The phone's battery was smaller than his current one.

Alessio frowned. "Huh. So they never actually said what it does better."

"Exactly. The famous person and the crowd did all the talking." Peyton felt that satisfying click of a pattern snapping into place, the same click she got when a math problem finally opened up. Ads weren't magic; they were doors with the hinges painted over.

Back in class, Ms. Ahmed asked them to design a poster about coastal erosion for the science fair, something that would make students care. "Make it persuasive but honest," she said.

Julian grinned and wrote, "Everyone is helping save the dunes." Peyton shook her head. "That's bandwagon, and it's not even true yet." They worked until the final bell, and when it rang she was still lettering her honest version: "The dunes are disappearing. Be competent, not just convinced."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never contained the metal lead; the name comes from early writers mistaking graphite for a kind of lead ore.
story:
George pressed his thumb against the sketch pad on the table, trying to keep the page from curling, but the jar of brushes someone had left in the middle of the workbench obstructed his view of the model still-life Mr. Whitehead had set up at the front of the studio. The community art studio smelled like turpentine and old erasers, and it was the only place in town where George felt like the things he made actually turned out the way he pictured them. Today he was drawing the still-life in pencil, because the graphite class project was due on Friday and he wanted the shading on the ceramic jug to look wet.

"Can I borrow your 6B?" Auston asked from the next stool. "Mine snapped. I sharpened it too hard."

George slid it across. "Just don't press down. The soft ones are brittle, so the tip breaks if you lean on it."

That was when Auston froze with the pencil halfway to his hand. "Wait. Is that lead? I'm not touching lead. My little brother got a splinter from a pencil last week and Mom said it would poison him. She made him drink milk."

"Lead poison," Colten said from across the table, nodding like an expert. "That's why they call it lead."

George remembered his own panic two summers ago, sitting on the back steps after stabbing his palm with a pencil point. His dad had found him sucking the wound and George had cried, certain he was going to get sick, and his dad had gone inside without answering and come back with an old science book and made him read one page aloud twice. George had slept fine that night, but he had never actually explained it to anyone else, and now both boys were looking at him like he either knew or didn't.

"It's not lead," George said. He reached for the box of pencils and turned it so they could read the side of one. "Look. It says graphite. Pencil lead has never actually been lead. The name stuck because early writers mistook graphite for a kind of lead ore." He tapped the box. "So your brother's splinter can't poison him. It's just dirty, like any splinter."

Auston picked up the 6B and turned it over slowly. "Never? Like, never ever?"

"That's what it says. Go ask Mr. Whitehead if you don't believe me."

Auston carried the pencil to the front of the room, and George watched him hold a whispered conversation with Mr. Whitehead, who smiled and nodded and pointed at the pencil with both hands like it was obvious. Auston came back walking taller. "He says the same thing. He says my mom is mixing it up with old paint." He sat down, tested the dark soft point on the corner of his page, and then leaned in and began blocking in the shadow under the jug.

George went back to his own drawing, and the pencil moved across the paper in long, certain strokes. "Tell your brother tomorrow," he said. "Tell him I said the milk part was the only useful thing your mom did."

Auston laughed and kept drawing, and the studio went quiet except for the sound of graphite, which was not lead, wearing down against paper.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story.
story:
Megan spread the short story across the kitchen table, smoothing the crease where she had folded it into her backpack. Her mom set a mug of cocoa beside her, warm enough that the chocolate smell reached Megan before she noticed the cup. "Thanks," Megan murmured, because tomorrow Ms. Holloway would call on someone to explain the story, and Megan badly wanted that someone to be ready.

The story was only eight pages, about a boy who kept seeing a red door at the end of a hallway he was never allowed to enter. Megan read it twice and still felt like she was standing outside it herself. Something about that door seemed to matter, but she could not say why, and Ms. Holloway would want more than a feeling.

Her phone buzzed. Brendan: book club at Xavier's, four o'clock, bring the story. Megan checked the clock, grabbed the pages, and ran the three blocks in the cold, her breath making little clouds that magnified in the frosty air before vanishing.

Xavier's basement smelled like popcorn. Brendan had already claimed the beanbag chair. "The red door means danger," he announced before Megan had her coat off. "Obviously."

"Obviously?" Xavier said. "Prove it from the text."

Brendan blinked. "It's red. Red means danger. Duh."

"That's not from the story, that's from stop signs." Megan dropped onto the couch and picked up her copy. Her instinct was to agree with Brendan, because the door did feel frightening, but a feeling was not the same as proof. She flipped pages, hunting. "Look. Page two, the father paints the door red the day he stops talking about the war. Page five, the boy's mother touches the door every time she says his brother's name. And the last page, when the boy finally opens it, there's just an empty room with his brother's boots in it."

Xavier leaned over her shoulder. "So the door isn't danger. It's the stuff nobody will talk about."

"Right." Megan tapped the page, her heart going quick. "A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself. But you have to support what you think it means with details from the story, or it's just guessing." She said it and then heard it, and it fit like a key turning.

Brendan sat up in the beanbag, deflating it with a sigh. "Fine. The red door is the family's silence. Three details, Megan, that's brutal." He said it admiringly, though.

"Also foreshadowing," Xavier said, spraying popcorn crumbs. "Every time the mom touches the door, it's hinting the brother is gone. Like breadcrumbs."

They worked until Mrs. Xavier's mother called down that it was almost dinner, and she brought a plate of cookies still soft in the middle, which felt like its own kind of small kindness. Megan copied the three page numbers onto a sticky note and pressed it inside her copy of the story, right next to the red door on the cover.

Walking home under the streetlights, she thought about the boots in the empty room, how something could stand for so much more than itself, and how you had to build the case detail by detail, like footprints leading somewhere you couldn't see from the start.

At the kitchen table the next morning, her mom slid the cocoa beside her again without being asked. Megan opened the story one last time, took a breath, and raised her hand the moment Ms. Holloway asked who wanted to go first.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
story:
Samanathan set the two bean pots side by side on the kitchen table and measured them again. The fertilized plant had grown two centimeters in five days. The unfertilized one had grown half that. She wrote the numbers in her lab notebook, then underlined her hypothesis twice, because so far the data agreed with it.

"Every single thing about these pots is supposed to be the same," she told Jolene, who had come over to see the project before the science fair. "Same soil, same amount of water, same kind of seed. Same size pot, too, I checked with the measuring cup. Equivalent in every way except one gets fertilizer and one doesn't."

"That's the point, right?" Jolene said. "A fair test. You change one thing, keep everything else the same, so you know the difference came from that one thing." She peered at the smaller plant and frowned. "This one looks kind of pale, though. Like my koala backpack when it got left in the rain. Poor sad marsupial."

Samantha lifted the pale pot to check the drainage holes, and that was when she noticed something odd. The table felt warm on one side. She turned her head slowly, the way you do when you don't want what you're about to see to be true. The bigger plant, the fertilized one, had been sitting directly in the afternoon sun from the window. The smaller pot stood in the shade of the cereal box tower her brother had left there on Tuesday. She checked her notebook. Tuesday was the day after she had planted the seeds.

"Jolene," she said quietly. "I've been giving the fertilizer plant sunlight too."

"So your results don't actually say anything about fertilizer," Jolene said. "They might just say that plants like sun, which, honestly, everyone already knows."

"It contradicts the whole project," Samantha said. Her stomach dropped. The science fair was in four days. She moved both pots to the middle of the table, drew a line between them with masking tape so she would remember to swap their positions every morning, and started a fresh page in the notebook. Day one, round two. Then she watered both plants with exactly thirty milliliters each, measuring twice, and carried the pots to the window shelf where the light fell evenly across both of them.

Jolene tapped the tape line with her toe. "So which one is which now?"

"The left one gets fertilizer this time," Samantha said. She uncapped the small bottle and bent over the left pot.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The group chat was supposed to be for the science fair, and for three days it mostly was. Then someone created a poll titled "Whose project is secretly the worst?" and by 9:04 p.m. Sophie's name was winning. She stared at her phone. The vote came from Mustafa, who sat beside her in homeroom and always shared his orange wedges at lunch.

"That poll is a joke," Mustafa said the next morning, holding out his orange like nothing had happened. "Everyone knows it's a joke."

Sophie took a wedge but kept her eyes on him. "You wrote under it, 'Sophie's volcano is a lava-fraud.' That's a whole sentence. That's not a joke sentence, that's a mean sentence."

"That's not me," Mustafa said. "That's chat me. Chat me has no manners."

That was the part Sophie couldn't stop turning over. Mustafa in person opened doors for teachers. Mustafa in the chat wrote things that would make his own grandmother ground him. It was the same thumbs typing both ways, so something invisible had to be in between. She had a theory, and she decided to test it right there in the chat, because theories deserve evidence.

She posted: "New rule. Anybody who wants to say something rude in here has to say it out loud to the person's face first. I'll wait."

Bruce replied with a row of crying-laughing faces. Then, ten minutes later, he walked up to her locker, cleared his throat, went pink, and said, "I, um. Your volcano is. A lava-fraud." It came out at the volume of a mosquito apologizing.

"Wow," Sophie said. "You couldn't even do it."

"I did do it," Bruce said, but he was laughing, and so was she, and Mustafa looked like he wanted the floor to accommodate him by swallowing him whole.

Ms. Jung caught the tail end of it when they filed into science. "Volcano fraud?" she asked, raising one eyebrow. Sophie showed her the poll, expecting a lecture. Instead Ms. Jung said, "Ah. The online disinhibition effect," and kept walking.

"The what?" Sophie ran after her. "Is that a spell?"

"Look it up," said Ms. Jung, which was the most teacher thing she could possibly say, so Sophie did, at lunch, with Mustafa reading over her shoulder. A psychologist named John Suler had written about it in 2004. People often said things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. That was it, the invisible thing between Mustafa's thumbs and his manners. Sophie felt almost disappointed it had a name, because her theory had been pretty credible.

"So chat me is real me with the brakes off," Mustafa said slowly. "That's horrifying. That's a humiliation machine with wifi."

"Then we fix the machine," Sophie said. She pulled out her phone and typed while they watched: "Poll results deleted. Replacement poll: whose orange wedges are the best? Winner gets my lava, fraud or not."

Mustafa voted for himself instantly. Twice.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
story:
The bus to Camp Wyoka left the canoe launch at ten sharp, which gave Bennett exactly forty minutes to decide whether to get on it. His duffel sat on the gravel next to a stack of rental canoes, and his father was pretending to check the tires so Bennett could have his crisis in private. Bennett's crisis was simple: three weeks away, no canoeing experience, and a packing list that included something called a "ditty bag," which he suspected was a joke the camp played on first-timers.

Cayden pedaled up on his bike, skidding gravel in a way that was clearly meant as a grand entrance. "My mom says I have to see you off," he announced, "so consider yourself seen." He handed Bennett a folded note. "Don't read it till you're on the bus. Rule of drama." Bennett put it in his pocket, and the two of them wandered down to the water, where Moussa was already failing to help a man load a canoe onto a roof rack. Moussa's family came to the launch every Saturday, and Moussa had explained canoe technique to Bennett at least six times, none of which had stuck.

"So what if you hate it?" Cayden asked, watching a dragonfly. "You can't just leave."

"I can write to you and you can fake a family emergency," Bennett said, though he had been reasoning through a different problem all morning. Camp Wyoka was accredited; he'd seen the sign at the gate when they registered him online, a badge he'd never questioned until his mother said, " Accredited by whom, exactly?" like it was a trick question. Nobody at home knew. He'd decided the bus would be his laboratory: if the camp was official enough to have standards, some adult there would know, and if nobody knew, that would tell him something too.

At ten sharp, a counselor named Mr. Boateng climbed off the bus and started counting heads. Bennett, carrying his duffel, nodded at the badge on the man's shirt. "That's the same seal as the sign. Who are you people, actually?"

Mr. Boateng looked pleased to be asked. "We're held to common standards for organized camps," he said. "It started in 1910, when it was called the Camp Directors Association of America. It's the American Camp Association now."

"Like a hundred years of adults checking on other adults," Bennett said.

"Basically," said Mr. Boateng, and moved on to counting Moussa, who had decided at the last minute to come after all and was arguing with his mother about a duffel of his own.

Bennett took a window seat and unfolded Cayden's note. "Dear Bennett," it read. "If they make you do trust falls, cease all trust immediately. Also, don't be a stereotype and write me one sad letter on day two. A contemporary of mine did that last summer and his friend still brings it up. P.S. I looked up your camp. It's legit. Check the sign." Bennett looked out the window at the badge by the gate, then waved at his father, who was still crouched by the tires, pretending the crisis had never happened.

"Day two," Bennett muttered, folding the note. "I'm aiming for day four."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
Felix stared at the group chat on his phone, thumb hovering. Alvin had posted a screenshot of the league scoring rankings with the caption "Case closed. Titans are the best team, end of story." Twelve thumbs-up followed, including one from Max, which stung, because Felix had actually watched the Titans play twice and both times they had gotten lucky in the last minute.

"They won five games by one point," Felix typed. "Is that the best team, or the luckiest?"

"Luck isn't a stat," Alvin replied.

Felix flopped onto his bed and thought about Saturday. He had been at a sports bar with his dad and his uncle, and between innings his uncle had leaned over and said, "You know, back in 2003 a guy named Michael Lewis wrote a book called Moneyball. It was about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics, stuff like on-base percentage, to find undervalued players." His uncle had shaken his head, smiling. "They didn't have the revenue to buy stars like the rich teams did. So they found players everybody else was ignoring."

"Undervalued how?" Felix had asked.

"The numbers said those players were better than anybody thought. One number told the whole story that the scouts kept missing."

Felix scrolled back through the chat now, wondering. If one number could hide a player's real worth, could a ranking hide a team's? He opened the league site and started digging. The Titans were first in points. But when he pulled up the game-by-game log, he found they had lost every match against teams above .500. They had fattened their record on the weakest opponents. Was that the best team, or the best schedule? He copied the results into his notes app, checking each one twice, because if he posted this and got it wrong, Alvin would never let it go.

He pasted a table into the chat: Titans against winning teams, 0 wins, 4 losses. Against losing teams, 9 and 1. Then he added one line. "Ranking is one number squishing nine games together. Squish different, get a different answer."

For a full minute nobody typed anything. Felix watched the three dots appear and vanish, appear and vanish. Max finally sent a single message: "Okay that's actually wild. Wait, does this mean my fantasy draft is wrong too?"

"Send me your list," Felix typed. "I'll squish it."
